introduction-list-price-is-for-retail.core: Public cloud prices are retail. Large, predictable spenders negotiate wholesale terms (EDPs, private pricing, credits) by offering commitment and volume.

first_principles.problem: A company spending $15M a year pays list price because nobody thought to negotiate.
derivation: Use an **EDP** for an overall discount.
Draw down through the **marketplace**; manage the **lifecycle**.

analogy.title: Costco vs. the corner shop
analogy.story: A restaurant buying 10,000 bottles gets wholesale prices a single shopper never sees.
analogy.breaks: Commitments create obligations, and over-committing leads to penalties.

example.title: First negotiation

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Large savings from a contract, not from engineering.

example.outcome: spend is bought at wholesale terms.

check.q: What do cloud providers want in exchange for discounts?
check.a: Committed, predictable spend over multiple years.

the-edp-enterprise-discount-program.core: An EDP (AWS; Azure EA/MACC, GCP commits) commits to a total spend over 1–5 years in exchange for a percentage discount across almost all services. Shortfalls are still billed.

first_principles.problem: Teams don't know how much to commit or what happens if usage falls short.
truths: Discount scales with commitment size and term.
The commitment is a floor you pay regardless.

analogy.title: A mobile plan with a minimum annual spend
analogy.story: You get a discount on every call but pay the minimum even in quiet months.
analogy.breaks: Discounts typically exclude some items (marketplace fees, some support).

example.title: Sizing a ramped EDP

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: A good discount with low shortfall risk.

example.outcome: commitments that save without trapping you.

check.q: What happens if you spend less than your EDP commitment?
check.a: You're still billed for the shortfall up to the committed amount.

private-pricing-agreements-ppa.core: A PPA negotiates a custom unit price for one high-volume service (S3 storage per TB, CloudFront egress per GB) beyond the flat EDP discount. It's where a large single-service spend gets its biggest savings.

first_principles.problem: A video company's CloudFront egress is 40% of its bill, and a flat EDP discount barely touches it.
derivation: Request **custom tiered rates** (per GB or TB).

analogy.title: A bulk-shipping contract with a courier
analogy.story: A store shipping 1M parcels a month negotiates a custom per-parcel rate.
analogy.breaks: PPAs come with volume commitments, and usage shifts can strand them.

example.title: Egress PPA

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: The largest single line item is cut sharply.

example.outcome: dominant costs are priced for your scale.

check.q: How does a PPA differ from an EDP?
check.a: A PPA sets custom unit pricing for a specific service, while an EDP gives a flat percentage discount across the whole bill.

negotiation-levers-what-do-cloud-provide.core: Providers want predictable committed revenue, growth (migrations onto their platform), strategic logos and case studies, adoption of newer services, and to win against competitors. Each one is a lever for you.

first_principles.problem: Customers negotiate on price alone and leave most of their leverage unused.
derivation: Show **competitive alternatives**; time the deal to **quarter-end**.

analogy.title: Buying a car at month-end
analogy.story: Salespeople with targets give better deals, and mentioning a competing dealer's offer helps.
analogy.breaks: Bluffing about switching clouds damages trust if it isn't credible.

example.title: Packaging a deal
example.outcome: negotiations capture value beyond the headline discount.

check.q: Name two non-price levers in cloud negotiations.
check.a: For example, agreeing to a public case study or bringing a large migration workload.

the-marketplace-hack-edp-drawdown-via-th.core: Buying third-party software (Datadog, Snowflake, MongoDB Atlas) through the cloud marketplace usually counts toward your EDP commitment, so spend you'd make anyway retires the commitment and consolidates billing.

first_principles.problem: A company is behind on its EDP burn-down while paying SaaS vendors directly outside the commitment.
truths: Marketplace purchases are billed through the cloud provider.
Providers often count eligible marketplace spend toward commitments.
derivation: Use **private offers** to keep negotiated vendor pricing.

analogy.title: Buying gift cards that count toward a loyalty target
analogy.story: Purchases you'd make anyway help you hit the tier that unlocks your discount.
analogy.breaks: Drawdown is often capped, and some listings aren't eligible.

example.title: Rescuing a shortfall
flow: Move Datadog + Snowflake renewals to marketplace private offers

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: No penalty and no extra spend.

example.outcome: SaaS purchases double as commitment burn-down.

check.a: A custom, negotiated price from a vendor delivered through the cloud marketplace, often counting toward commitments.

contract-lifecycle-management-negotiatio.core: Manage cloud contracts continuously: prepare 6–12 months before renewal, track burn-down and usage monthly, renegotiate on major changes, and use quarterly business reviews with the account team.

first_principles.problem: Renewals are rushed in the last month, with no data and no leverage, and the old terms roll over.
derivation: **Prepare**: forecast and benchmark 6–12 months before renewal.

analogy.title: Managing a long-term lease
analogy.story: Track usage, talk with the landlord, and start renegotiating well before it expires.
analogy.breaks: Mid-term renegotiation isn't always possible, so build flexibility in up front.

example.title: A renewal timeline

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Better terms and no last-minute panic.

example.outcome: contracts are an ongoing FinOps discipline.
